name: Profit per customer against its cost
idea: An essay on subscription software states that a great way to understand any business model is to ask whether more profit can be made from customers than it costs to acquire them, using the lifetime value of a typical customer and the cost to acquire one. It states that the best such businesses have a ratio above 3, and that many of the best recover the cost to acquire in 5-7 months.
suggests: Look at what a typical customer brings in over its life, what it costs to win one, and how long it takes to earn that cost back, for each kind of customer separately.
limits: The essay stresses that its ratios are only guidelines and that entrepreneurs are usually overoptimistic about the cost of winning a customer. An executive of a software company quoted in it says that working out the ratio by segment can be hard, especially the cost side.
competing_idea: A magazine article reporting a paper states that, according to the paper's authors, a lifetime-value calculation must take margin, retention rate and the discount rate into account. It adds that an investor company able to calculate it and forecast customer numbers can gauge a company's customer base.
questions: What does a typical customer bring in over its life, and what does it cost to win and serve one?
How long does it take for a customer to repay what it cost to acquire?
Do some kinds of customer repay their cost much faster than others?

originals.reference: David Skok, "SaaS Metrics 2.0 - A Guide to Measuring and Improving what Matters", forEntrepreneurs.com, undated online article
Lauren Keller Johnson, "The Real Value of Customer Loyalty", MIT Sloan Management Review, 15 January 2002
originals.about: Sunil Gupta and Donald R. Lehmann, "Customers as Assets", working paper, Columbia Business School, August 2001
